title: In 200 Seats, the ECI Has No Record of How Many Citizens Voted After 5 PM in 2024 Elections
shows: It concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In Part 2 of its Election Audit series, the Reporters' Collective reports that it read the Election Commission's internal reports of the returning officers for 530 Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir that voted in 2024, and that in 200 of them the reports carry no count of votes polled after 5 pm. It gives these as 114 of Maharashtra's 288 Assembly seats, 44 of Jammu and Kashmir's 90 and 22 of Haryana's 90, with 18 of Maharashtra's 48 Lok Sabha seats and one each in Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir. It says the Commission's rules require the presiding officer to note the votes on the machine every two hours and tally them against the register of voters, and that in 23 seats the number of slips handed to voters still in the queue at the close of poll was not recorded. In the 174 Maharashtra Assembly seats where the count was recorded, it finds 50.87 lakh votes cast after 5 pm. It says it does not conclude whether or where voting was rigged. The Chief Electoral Officers of Haryana, Jammu and Kashmir and Maharashtra answered on X on 18 November that the Commission publishes the votes polled in its index cards, that Form 17C is the statutory account given to the polling agents at the close of poll, that the returning officer's report is a non-statutory summary, and that no separate statutory record of polling after 5 pm exists. In a thread on 19 November one of the reporters, Sumedha Mittal, called that answer misleading and said the missing figures are the two-hourly counts from the presiding officer's diary, which reach the Commission's headquarters through the returning officer's report.
quote: New Delhi: In 200 constituencies that went to either parliamentary or assembly polls in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu & Kashmir in 2024, the Election Commission of India (ECI) failed to record how many people voted after 5 pm.
We do not conclude whether or where voting was rigged.
note: First reading, 21 November 2026. Read in full from the Collective's page with curl on 21 November 2026, reached from the homepage because the sitemap and the story listing answer Not Found. The page prints no date. The date is 18 November from Sumedha Mittal's post on X of that day at 03:42 UTC (9:12 am IST) announcing the story, and the Haryana reply of 18 November names it. The Collective's own account posted on 17 November at 14:54 UTC that Part 2 would appear the next day at 8:30 am. Byline Sumedha Mittal and Venkatesh Nayak, edited by Furquan Ameen. Every figure in the summary is in the article as written. The seat counts add up: 114, 44 and 22 Assembly seats and 18, 1 and 1 Lok Sabha seats make 200, and the 530 are the 467 Assembly and 63 Lok Sabha seats the article says it read, with the report for Devsar in Jammu and Kashmir not found. The article is about the 2024 polls and holds no figure on the electoral rolls, so nothing in it can be checked against the site's data, and every figure is the Collective's. The Commission's side is listed separately from the Chief Electoral Officer of Haryana's post on X of 18 November (x.com/ceoharyana/status/2122967800071487886, four pages read as images). The Jammu and Kashmir post of the same day (x.com/ceo_UTJK/status/2122958954045345973) is a card carrying the first six points and the word misleading. Maharashtra's reply of 18 November was seen only as a screenshot in the reporter's thread, because its account could not be fetched, and its card carries the same six points. The reporter's thread (x.com/TweetSumedha/status/2123365076522672366, 20 numbered posts and a correction, 19 November) was read in full through api.fxtwitter.com. Her thread's account of an RTI reply on the slips is not carried. Not carried either are the article's account of the Kopri-Pachpakhadi seat, which names the candidates and works out a rate of voting per minute, its quotation of the Chief Election Commissioner on CCTV footage, the former Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa's comments, the article's description of the evening hours as open to bogus voting, which it attributes to unnamed experts, and the opposition's claim of 76 lakh votes after 5 pm in Maharashtra. The Collective's Part 1 of 10 November, on votes polled against votes counted, is also about the 2024 polls and is not listed.

title: Factual Position regarding report published on reporters-collective.in
shows: It concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In a four-page note posted on 18 November, in reply to the Reporters' Collective's report that the returning officers' reports for 200 seats in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir carry no count of votes polled after 5 pm, the Chief Electoral Officer of Haryana says that the Commission publishes the electors, the votes polled on the machines and by post and the turnout of every seat in its index cards, which are generated by the system from the records made at polling and counting. It says the presiding officer records the total of votes polled in Form 17C at the close of poll and gives a copy to every polling agent present. It describes the returning officer's report as an administrative narrative of the conduct of the poll, drawn from the presiding officer's diary and other papers, filled in by hand and non-statutory, and says that a divergence between the two is a difference in the design of the two reporting formats and no evidence of wrongdoing. It says no separate statutory record of polling after 5 pm exists, that the final figure is recorded at the close of poll and at no fixed clock time, and that the register of voters, the presiding officer's diary and other papers are scrutinised on the day after the poll so that a repoll can be recommended where needed. The Chief Electoral Officer of Jammu and Kashmir posted the first six points the same day on a card that calls the report misleading. In a thread on 19 November one of the Collective's reporters, Sumedha Mittal, called the reply misleading and said the missing figures are the two-hourly counts from the presiding officer's diary, which reach the Commission's headquarters through the returning officer's report.
quote: No such separate statutory record exists. Under the law, the final figure of votes polled is recorded at the Close of Poll, not at any fixed clock time.
The chain behind the Index Card is statutory and verifiable; the RO Report is a non-statutory summary.
note: First reading, 21 November 2026. The post of 18 November 2026 at 08:19 UTC (1:49 pm IST), read through api.fxtwitter.com, and its four attached pages (pbs.twimg.com/media/HXZL4eGaoAAMqlA, HXZL4h2a4AEGoEV, HXZL4ebacAAJEcI and HXZL4eia0AA4zT6) read as images, in the order posted, pages 1 to 4 of 4. The post's text reads '#FACTCHECKFactual Position regarding report published on https://reporters-collective.in with heading “ Part 2, Election Audit, In 200 seats, the ECI has no records of how many citizens voted after 5 pm in 2024 Elections”@reporters_co', and the title here is its words from Factual to the address. The note is unsigned and is the Haryana office's post, under which X shows the label Election Commission of India and Spokesperson ECI, so it is listed as the Commission's account. Both quotes are verbatim from page 1. Point 4 of the note reads 'A divergence between the two is a difference of design of the two reporting formats, not evidence of wrong doing' and does not say which two records it means, so the summary keeps its wording. The note's worked examples (polling hours of 7 am to 4 pm in Meghalaya in February 2023, and a queue of 120 voters at 45 seconds each) are not carried. The Chief Electoral Officer of Jammu and Kashmir posted at 07:43 UTC the same day (x.com/ceo_UTJK/status/2122958954045345973) a card headed Claim, Fact and Misleading carrying points 1 to 6, whose first point adds that index cards are published within 72 hours of the results and whose fourth names the sector magistrate's report among the returning officer's sources. Maharashtra's reply of 18 November, a card with the same six points, was seen only as a screenshot in the reporter's thread, because the office's account could not be fetched. The reporter's thread (x.com/TweetSumedha/status/2123365076522672366, 20 numbered posts and a correction, 19 November 10:37 UTC) was read in full through api.fxtwitter.com, and her account of it is attributed to her. The article itself is listed under Investigations. The dispute concerns the 2024 polls, so neither side's account can be checked against the site's roll data.

title: Transgender Voters Are Disappearing From Electoral Rolls at More Than Twice the Overall Rate
shows: Vaivab Das, a doctoral scholar at IIT Delhi, writes in The Wire on the Transgender Day of Remembrance that electors registered as transgender fell much faster than the electorate in 12 states and union territories. By the article's own tabulation of the Election Commission's statistical records and the summaries the Chief Electoral Officers released, electors in Assam, Bihar, Delhi, Goa, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Odisha, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal fell from 62.6 crore to 55.1 crore, or 11.91%, while transgender electors fell from 35,870 to 24,811, or 30.8%. It gives the largest falls as Delhi (65%), Maharashtra (49%), Karnataka (43%) and Uttar Pradesh (37%). The article's set includes Assam, which had a Special Revision in place of the intensive one, and where its table shows the whole roll growing. The article labels its earlier figures 2024 or 2025. Its later totals for Delhi, Maharashtra and Karnataka equal their draft rolls and its later total for Odisha equals Odisha's final roll, so its falls set drafts beside final rolls. It also sets the 2024 Lok Sabha rolls against the 2011 Census count of transgender persons. It quotes a trans masculine person working in Bengaluru, under a changed name, who says that after he applied using his parents' entry in the 2002 roll a notice told him his name and his father's name did not match, and that the booth level officer then asked for his father's documents although he has not been in touch with his family for ten years. The author argues that tying enrolment to the family puts at risk the vote of transgender people who have left their families.
quote: Across the 12 states and union territories examined, registered transgender electors declined by approximately 30.84%, compared to an overall decline of 11.92%.
Their numbers fell from 35,870 to 24,811, a reduction of 30.8%, which is more than 2.5 times the overall percentage decline.
note: First reading, 21 November 2026. Published 20 November 2026 at 2:23 pm IST (post_date 2026-11-20 14:23:39), read in full from The Wire's content API (cms.thewire.in/wp-json/thewire/v2/posts/detail) with curl on 21 November 2026, and the public address above answers 200. Free to read. The author is described at the foot as a PhD scholar at IIT Delhi and a Fulbright Nehru Doctoral Fellow at the University of California, Berkeley. The state table is an image (cms.thewire.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/VD6.png), read with the Read tool. Every figure in the summary is The Wire's. The article prints the overall fall as 11.91% in the text and 11.92% in the standfirst and chart, and the transgender fall as 30.8% in the text and table and 30.84% in the standfirst and chart. Its own totals, 62,60,32,530 to 55,14,62,374 and 35,870 to 24,811, work out to 11.91% and 30.83%. The state falls of 65%, 49%, 43% and 37% are rounded from its table (64.7%, 49.4%, 42.7%, 36.6%). Checked against the site. data/india/raw/third_gender.csv holds only West Bengal, with 1,777 third gender electors on the roll of 27 October 2025 and 1,402 on the draft, and The Wire's table gives West Bengal 1,773 before and 1,257 after, so its West Bengal figures are on other rolls from the site's. The Wire's later totals equal the site's drafts for Delhi (97,53,577), Maharashtra (7,71,65,562) and Karnataka (4,46,35,975), which are electors_before less the names left off in data/india/states.json. Delhi's and Maharashtra's final rolls are due on 22 December, and Karnataka's final roll of 27 October (4,54,55,689) is not the one used. The later total equals the site's final roll for Odisha (3,16,32,754). Uttar Pradesh's later total in the table is 13,39,84,802, 10 more than the site's final roll of 13,39,84,792, and its row adds up to that figure. For Bihar, Kerala, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal the later totals match neither the site's draft nor its final roll. Goa's later total, 5,59,282, is about half of the 10,57,566 on its final roll in states.json, and that figure is The Wire's and is not explained. Its baselines also differ from the site's rolls before the revision (Delhi 1,56,26,736 against 1,45,10,299, for instance), so the article's state falls are not comparable with the site's counts of names left off. Assam is in no table of the site's revision states. process.json (timeline step 'Assam gets a different revision') says Assam was given a Special Revision in place of an intensive one, with a final roll due on 10 February 2026, and The Wire's table shows Assam's roll rising from 2,45,72,114 to 2,51,17,886 while its transgender electors fell from 404 to 318. The table's later female total is 26,62,43,100 while its rows add to 26,62,43,080, because West Bengal's men, women and transgender electors add to 6,83,62,013 against a printed total of 6,83,62,033. Neither figure is carried. The overall fall the summary gives, 11.91%, is the one the totals support. The person quoted from Bengaluru is a private person under a changed name and is described by role only. The article's quotations of activists, its account of the Election Commission's past outreach to transgender voters, its arguments on citizenship law and on the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act 2026, and its remarks on the government are the author's and are not carried.
